scenes.name: John Coltrane
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Músico tardío y obsesivo del ensayo, pasa por Gillespie, Hodges, el quinteto de Miles y el Five Spot con Monk antes de afirmarse con Blue Train (1957). Ira Gitler habla de sus «capas de sonido»: cascadas de notas, escalas y arpegios. Giant Steps (1959) es el arquetipo del jazz de acordes a toda velocidad; enseguida gira hacia lo modal («My Favorite Things»), pero con escalas superpuestas sobre bajos estáticos, estructuras bizantinas que McCoy Tyner (cuartas sin resolver, un tsunami sonoro) y Elvin Jones sostienen. En Impulse alterna discos accesibles (Ballads, con Johnny Hartman, con Ellington) con blues imposibles, «Alabama», A Love Supreme (1965) y, al final, el free de Ascension y Meditations con Alice Coltrane y Rashied Ali. Lector de Krishnamurti y de Slonimsky, curioso por la India y África, recupera el saxo soprano. Muere en 1967.
scenes.family: Hard bop, soul jazz y post-bop

podcast.title: Approves "That'll Be the Day" for Release (1957)
podcast.body: When Norman Petty shopped the recordings for "That'll Be the Day," Bob Thiele immediately recognized their quality, stating they were "fine as it was" and approved them for release as a Brunswick group. "But the Crickets had still not properly finalised their lineup. The Core of Holly and Allison was there."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode Sixty-One: "That'll Be the Day", by the Crickets

podcast.title: Decca Executive for Subsidiaries (1957)
podcast.body: Thiele was brought on by Decca, which recognized his understanding of the changing music business, and was placed in charge of two of Decca's labels: Coral, used for "insipid white cover versions of Black Acts," and Brunswick, dedicated to rockabilly tracks. "He'd been put in charge of two labels on by Decker. The Cuddle, which was being used mostly for insipid white cover versions of Black Acts, and Bunswick, which was where he released Rockabilly Tracks by Johnny Benett and the Rock and Roll trio."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Producer of "What A Wonderful World" (1967)
podcast.body: Bob Thiele was the producer who, along with songwriter George David Weiss, offered the orchestral pop ballad "What A Wonderful World" to Louis Armstrong in 1967. "Three years later, Armstrong was offered an orchestral pop ballad about the wonders of existence by producer Bob Feel and songwriter George David Weiss."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Career Path Similar to Milt Gabler
podcast.body: Bob Thiele had a career trajectory similar to Milt Gabler, beginning as a musician, then founding his own specialty jazz label, Signature, and producing significant jazz records like Coleman Hawkins' "The Man I Love." "Old had had a similar career to Milt Gabler. He'd start about as a musician, then he'd found his own speciality jazz label, Signature, and to produce records like Coleman Hawkins' The Man I Love."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
